dn14:1.32.4: the wheel, the elephant, the horse, the jewel, the woman, the householder, and the commander as the seventh treasure.

dn14:1.32.6: After conquering this land girt by sea, he reigns by principle, without rod or sword.

dn14:2.3.6: Seeing this, he said to me:

dn14:2.3.8: “That, Your Majesty, is called an old man.”
dn14:2.3.9: “But why is he called an old man?”
dn14:2.3.10: “He’s called an old man because now he has not long to live.”
dn14:2.3.11: “But my dear charioteer, am I liable to grow old? Am I not exempt from old age?”
dn14:2.3.12: “Everyone is liable to grow old, Your Majesty, including you. No one is exempt from old age.”
dn14:2.3.13: “Well then, my dear charioteer, that’s enough of the park for today. Let’s return to the royal compound.”
dn14:2.3.14: “Yes, Your Majesty,” I replied to the prince, Your Majesty, and did so.
dn14:2.3.15: Back at the royal compound, Your Majesty, the prince brooded, miserable and sad:
dn14:2.3.16: “Curse this thing called rebirth, since old age will come to anyone who’s born.”’

dn14:3.19.1: The Buddha Vipassī taught them step by step, with
dn14:3.19.2: a talk on giving, ethical conduct, and heaven. He revealed the drawbacks of sensual pleasures, so sordid and corrupt, and the benefit of renunciation.
dn14:3.19.3: And when he knew that their minds were ready, pliable, rid of hindrances, elated, and confident he revealed the special teaching of the Buddhas:
dn14:3.19.4: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

dn14:3.19.6: in that very seat the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in those 84,000 who had gone forth:

dn14:3.20.3: As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, the Buddha has made the teaching clear in many ways.

dn14:3.23.5: “Wander forth, mendicants, for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
dn14:3.23.6: Let not two go by one road.
dn14:3.23.7: Teach the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.
dn14:3.23.8: There are beings with little dust in their eyes. They’re in decline because they haven’t heard the teaching. There will be those who understand the teaching!”
dn14:3.24.2: ‘Mendicants, as I was in private retreat this thought came to my mind:
dn14:3.24.3: “The Saṅgha residing at Bandhumatī now is large.
dn14:3.24.4: What if I was to urge them:
dn14:3.24.5: Wander forth, mendicants, for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
dn14:3.24.6: Let not two go by one road.
dn14:3.24.7: Teach the Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.
dn14:3.24.8: There are beings with little dust in their eyes. They’re in decline because they haven’t heard the teaching. There will be those who understand the teaching!
dn14:3.24.9: But when six years have passed, you must all come to Bandhumatī to recite the monastic code.”’
dn14:3.25.1: Then a certain Great Divinity, knowing my train of thought, as easily as a strong person would extend or contract their arm, vanished from the realm of divinity and reappeared in front of me.
dn14:3.25.2: He arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward me, and said,
dn14:3.25.3: ‘That’s so true, Blessed One! That’s so true, Holy One!
dn14:3.25.4: The Saṅgha residing at Bandhumatī now is large.
dn14:3.25.6: Wander forth, mendicants, for the welfare and happiness of the people, out of sympathy for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
dn14:3.25.7: Let not two go by one road.
dn14:3.25.9: There are beings with little dust in their eyes. They’re in decline because they haven’t heard the teaching. There will be those who understand the teaching!
dn14:3.25.10: And sir, I’ll make sure that when six years have passed the mendicants will return to Bandhumatī to recite the monastic code.’
dn14:3.25.11: That is what that Great Divinity said.
dn14:3.25.12: Then he bowed and respectfully circled me, keeping me on his right, before vanishing right there.
dn14:3.31.4: ‘Ninety-one eons ago, good fellow, the Buddha Vipassī arose in the world, perfected and fully awakened.
dn14:3.31.5: He was born as an aristocrat.
dn14:3.31.6: He arose in an aristocrat family.
dn14:3.31.9: He was awakened at the root of a patala tree.
dn14:3.31.10: He had a fine pair of chief disciples named Khaṇḍa and Tissa.
dn14:3.31.11: He had three gatherings of disciples.
dn14:3.31.12: One gathering of disciples was of 6,800,000 mendicants.
dn14:3.31.13: One gathering of disciples was of 100,000 mendicants.
dn14:3.31.14: One gathering of disciples was of 80,000 mendicants.
dn14:3.31.15: These were the Buddha Vipassī’s three gatherings of disciples, all of them mendicants who had ended their defilements.
dn14:3.31.16: He had as chief attendant a mendicant named Asoka.
dn14:3.31.17: His father was King Bandhumā, his birth mother was Queen Bandhumatī,
dn14:3.31.18: and their capital city was named Bandhumatī.
dn14:3.31.19: And such was his renunciation, such his going forth, such his striving, such his awakening, and such his rolling forth of the Wheel of Dhamma.
dn14:3.31.20: And good fellow, after leading the spiritual life under that Buddha Vipassī we lost our desire for sensual pleasures and were reborn here.’
dn14:3.31.21: In that order of gods, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of deities approached me, bowed, stood to one side, and said to me,
dn14:3.31.22: ‘Thirty-one eons ago, good fellow, the Buddha Sikhī …
dn14:3.31.23: we, good fellow, under the Buddha Sikhī; in the same thirty-first eon, good fellow, the Buddha Vessabhū …
dn14:3.31.24: we, good fellow, under the Buddha Vessabhū …
dn14:3.31.25: In the present fortunate eon, good fellow, the Buddhas Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa …
dn14:3.31.26: And good fellow, after leading the spiritual life under the Buddhas Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa we lost our desire for sensual pleasures and were reborn here.’
dn14:3.32.1: In that order of gods, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of deities approached me, bowed, stood to one side, and said to me,
dn14:3.32.2: ‘In the present fortunate eon, good fellow, you have arisen in the world, perfected and fully awakened.
dn14:3.32.3: You were born as an aristocrat into an aristocrat family.
dn14:3.32.5: For you the lifespan is short, brief, and fleeting. A long life is a hundred years or a little more.
dn14:3.32.6: You were awakened at the root of a peepal tree.
dn14:3.32.7: You have a fine pair of chief disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
dn14:3.32.8: You have had one gathering of disciples—1,250 mendicants.
dn14:3.32.9: This one gathering of disciples consisted entirely of mendicants who had ended their defilements.
dn14:3.32.10: You have as chief attendant a mendicant named Ānanda.
dn14:3.32.12: your birth mother was Queen Māyā,
dn14:3.32.13: and your capital city was Kapilavatthu.
dn14:3.32.14: And such was your renunciation, such your going forth, such your striving, such your awakening, and such your rolling forth of the Wheel of Dhamma.
dn14:3.32.15: And good fellow, after leading the spiritual life under you we lost our desire for sensual pleasures and were reborn here.’
